Chapter 6: Disrupting Unhelpful Patterns and Creating New Habits
Now that you’ve started building momentum through action and accountability, let’s talk about what really helps you break free from old routines—disrupting patterns that just aren’t working for you, and replacing them with habits that actually move you forward.
You know, changing habits isn’t usually a one-and-done kind of thing. Think of it more like rewiring the way you move through life, step by step. Imagine your old habits as those trails in a field that everyone walks over and over—the grass gets trampled, and the path is easy to follow. To go somewhere new, you have to step off that familiar track and start forging a new trail. At first, it might feel weird or uncomfortable, but that’s just part of the process.
So, how do you actually disrupt those unhelpful patterns? There are two main moves here.
First, learn to interrupt your automatic response. The next time you catch yourself slipping into an old habit, try pausing for a second. Maybe take a deep breath, or quietly ask yourself, " Is this choice really taking me where I want to go?"
Second, instead of just trying to stop the behavior, swap it out for something that serves you better. Let’s say you usually grab your phone when you’re stressed. What if, instead, you tried a quick walk, or just a few minutes of mindful breathing? The idea is to meet the same need, but in a much healthier way.
It also helps to think ahead about situations that tend to trip you up. For example, if certain meetings leave you feeling defensive, make a plan for how you want to respond next time. Jot down a couple of new actions or phrases you can use when the moment comes.
And remember, small, steady changes are way easier to stick with than giant, dramatic overhauls. Every time you choose that new path, even if it’s just a little thing, you’re making it easier to do again. Over time, those small choices really add up—and before you know it, your default responses start to shift.
There’s a really useful tool for this called the " habit loop." Here’s how it works: Every habit has a cue—that’s what triggers it—a routine, which is the action you take, and a reward, which is the payoff you get. When you break down your habits this way, you can start to experiment. Keep the same cue and reward, but try changing the routine. For instance, if feeling overwhelmed usually leads you to avoid things, but the reward is relief, what if you swapped avoidance for a quick stretch or a supportive chat with someone you trust?
And don’t worry if you slip up. Setbacks are totally normal. If you fall back into an old pattern, treat it as a chance to learn—not a failure. Ask yourself, " What triggered me this time? What could I do differently next time?" Over the long run, a little self-compassion and steady persistence make it absolutely possible to reshape even your toughest habits.
